correctness.rationale: The exact 2020 source defines S_J=sum_i (Lambda_i*Lambda_i)^1/2 (tildeLambda_i*tildeLambda_i)^1/2 and S_J+S_Jc=K. With C=C’=I and Lambda_i=P_i, tildeLambda_i=Q_i=P_iR, four matrices are real symmetric positive definite (determinants 1,2,2,4; positive traces); R has determinant 2. Their representation ranges coincide exactly, allowing the paper’s domain-restricted synthesis operator to act on the tilde analysis vector. Matrix products give A=P1Q1=[[2,-4],[-3,7]], B=P2Q2=[[2,-6],[-4,16]], K=A+B=[[4,-10],[-7,23]], det K=22. Lambda is a K-g frame because P1²+P2² is positive definite. With f=(1,i), exact conjugate-first complex products give <Af,Bf>=152-24i and <Bf,Af>=152+24i; these equal the original theorem’s two sides. The complex equality is false. For any A+B=K, taking real parts gives Re<Af,Kf>-||Af||²=Re<Bf,Kf>-||Bf||² by conjugate symmetry; no finite extrapolation is used. The proof is specific to Theorem 3.2, not adjacent inequalities.

evidence: Forughi et al. (2019), arXiv:1905.08962v1, Section 4 Theorem 4.1 already presents an analogous equality for I-duals and section 2 defines synthesis/analysis on the representation range.
The 2020 Theorem 3.2 is the general-K extension, now with partial operators summing to K rather than I. The submitted K=([[4,-10],[-7,23]]) is nonidentity and nonself-adjoint.
